case_name: Re Janzen and Platy Enterprises Ltd.
text:
Janzen v. Platy Enterprises Ltd.

1986-11-19

Court of Appeal Decision under the
MANITOBA HUMAN RIGHTS ACT

Dianna Janzen

and

Tracy Govereau

(Complainants) Respondents

v.

Platy Enterprises Ltd.

and

Platy Enterprises Ltd. carrying on business under
the firm name and style of Pharos Restaurant

and

Tommy Grammas

(Respondents) Appellants

Date of Complaints:

1982

Date of Decision:

November 19, 1986

Place:

Winnipeg, Manitoba

Before:

Matas, Huban and Twaddle, JJ. A.

Appearances by:

G. Mitchell, Counsel for Dianna Janzen and Tracy Govereau

J. M. Scurfield and C. W. Martin, Counsel for Platy Enterprises Ltd.

SEXUAL HARASSMENT — definition of sexual harassment — LIABILITY — employer/corporate liability for manager — mitigation of effects of discrimination — vicarious liability — INTERPRETATION OF STATUTES — definition of "sexual harassment" — JURISDICTION —
Constitution Act, 1867,
s. 96

Summary:
The Court of Appeal rules that sexual harassment is not sex discrimination within the meaning of the Manitoba Human Rights Act.

This is an appeal by Platy Enterprises from a Court of Queen's Bench decision reported at
1985 CanLII 3070 (MB QB)
,
7 C.H.R.R. D/3309
, upholding the Board of Adjudication decision reported at
1985 CanLII 5235 (MB HRC)
,
6 C.H.R.R. D/2735
, which found that sexual harassment is sex discrimination and that Platy Enterprises Ltd. was liable for the sexual harassment of two waitresses by the cook in Pharos Restaurant, Tommy Grammas.

The Court of Appeal rules that sexual harassment is not sex discrimination because sexual harassment occurs because of the personal characteristics of a woman, not simply because of her gender. Sexual harassment is not a case in which an employer adopts a practice which treats women as a class differently from men. Nor is it a case in which a rule of general application affects women adversely. For harassment to amount to discrimination, it must occur by reason of the categorical selection of the complainants because they are women.

The Court also finds that the employer Platy Enterprises would not be liable for the acts of its cook, Tommy Grammas, even if the acts of harassment were contrary to the Act. Although the waitresses were told by the owner of the restaurant that Tommy Grammas had the authority to fire them, the Court finds that he did not harass the waitresses ”˜in the course of his employment'.

In order for an employer to be liable for the acts of its employees, these acts must be engaged in ”˜during the course of employment'. An employer will be liable for discrimination by an employee who has the authority to hire and discriminates in doing so. However, the Court rules that "(p)atting the buttocks of a waitress is dehors (the) job (of) a cook." Consequently, the employer is not liable.

The appeal is allowed.

[
1
]  Our former colleague, Matas J.A., did not participate in the preparation of reasons for judgment which follow. This decision, to allow the appeal, is made pursuant to
section 21
of
The
Court of Appeal Act,
C.C.S.M. cap. C-240.

Huband J.A.:

[
2
]  I am amazed to think that sexual harassment has been equated with discrimination on the basis of sex. I think they are entirely different concepts. But adjudicators under human rights legislation, legal scholars and writers, and jurists have said that the one is included in the other.

[
3
]  Assuming sexual harassment to be a form of sexual discrimination, I am amazed to think that an employer could be held vicariously responsible for that form of discrimination on the part of an employee, or that a corporate employer could be found "personally responsible" for a sexually malevolent employee, except under the rarest of circumstances. Yet adjudicators, legal scholars, and judges have said otherwise.

[
4
]  These are the crucial issues which are joined in this appeal.

The Facts:

[
5
]  Two complaints were processed under
The
Human Rights Act
of Manitoba,
C.C.S.M. c. H175
(the
Act
). The two complainants were waitresses in Pharos Restaurant located at 9 St. Mary's Road in Winnipeg. The restaurant was one of three in metropolitan Winnipeg owned by a corporation, Platy Enterprises Ltd. (Platy).

[
6
]  The miscreant in this whole affair was the cook. One Tommy Grammas was employed as cook at the St. Mary's Road location during the months of August through December of 1982 when the complaints arose. By the time of the adjudication under the
Act
,
Tommy the cook had long since disappeared. The whole point of the exercise was to affix the corporate employer with responsibility for Tommy the cook's aberrant amorous conduct.

[
7
]  The first complaint was by Dianna Janzen who was employed as a waitress in the restaurant from late August until the end of October, 1982. After a firs few uneventful weeks, Tommy the cook began to bother her. It took the form of touching the areas of her buttocks, her abdomen, or her breasts, at unexpected moments or at times when she was least capable of fending him off because of her duties. She protested, and after about a month Tommy seemed to get the intended message. Thereafter, he began to make life difficult for her  as a cook can do with a waitress who depends upon him to provide the orders on a timely basis. After a further two weeks Ms. Janzen quit her job to take employment in another restaurant where she had worked before, but not before a discussion with the manager of the restaurant, one Philip Anastasiadis (Philip).

[
8
]  Philip is one of three brothers who are the shareholders of Platy, and which in turn operates three restaurants in Winnipeg under the name Pharos. Philip was president and a director of the corporation and was the manager of the St. Mary's Road restaurant. He was responsible for all of the purchasing, the hiring, instruction, discipline and discharge of employees at that location, the keeping of accounts, and the payment of wages. He also did the cooking on the first shift, and was responsible for general oversight of the restaurant during that shift. A second shift began at 5:00 p.m. and continued until midnight. If the evening shift was not busy, part of the waitressing staff might be sent home early.

[
9
]  Tommy the cook was the person in charge during the evening shift when Philip was not present himself. Tommy had general oversight of the restaurant and its employees and he would decide whether to send employees home early and, if so, which employees would be released. He did not have the authority to hire or fire, but the waitresses did not know this. Indeed, Philip encouraged the staff to believe that in his absence, Tommy the cook had such authority.

[
10
]  Philip himself would return, regularly, to the restaurant near the end of the evening shift to calculate the day's accounts and to close up. The evidence discloses that if Tommy the cook was unavailable for some reason, Philip would work a full double shift.

[
11
]  There is no suggestion that Philip was ever present when Tommy the cook engaged in sexual harassment of staff members, or that he approbated such conduct.

[
12
]  About two weeks before she resigned, Ms. Janzen attempted to discuss the problem she was having with Tommy the cook with Philip. It was around that time that sexual harassment had stopped but Tommy was making things difficult for her in other ways. Ms. Janzen attempted to speak with Philip towards the end of an evening shift, but he was in a rush for some reason. He put Ms. Janzen off before giving her a chance to indicate the nature of her complaint. As he was leaving the premises, Ms. Janzen claims that he said, "If it is about Tommy, I can't do anything about it."

[
13
]  The matter was not pursued further until near the end of October. Philip drove Ms. Janzen home from work. She took the opportunity to tell him of her problem with Tommy the cook. Ms. Janzen and Philip have slightly different interpretations of the conversation. Ms. Janzen says that Philip was unsympathetic, and so she made the decision to resign at the end of the month. Philip claims that Ms. Janzen had given him notice to quit before raising the complaint about Tommy. He agrees that he told her that she was overreacting, but he promised to talk to Tommy. He offered to transfer Ms. Janzen to another Pharos Restaurant if she would feel more comfortable in different surroundings.

[
14
]  Philip says that he did in fact speak with Tommy who denied the validity of the complaint. In any event, sexual harassment of Ms. Janzen had ceased by this point. Philip says that he also called a staff meeting and inquired of other waitresses whether they had similar experiences or similar complaints. The adjudicator did not believe Philip's evidence on these points.

[
15
]  The second complaint was raised by Tracy Govereau who was also a waitress at the same restaurant. She joined the staff in mid-October, 1982, and ended her employment on December 11, 1982. At first she had no problems with Tommy the cook. But after about one week he began a pattern of sexual harassment very similar to that which had recently ended with Ms. Janzen. There were attempted kisses, and unwelcomed pats, hugs and suggestive remarks. This conduct continued until about mid-November. At the instigation of another sympathetic waitress, Ms. Govereau complained to Philip. The discussion lasted about fifteen minutes. Thereafter the sexual harassment on the part of Tommy the cook ceased, but Tommy the cook and Philip made life difficult for her in another fashion. She said they were demanding, and unjustly critical of her work.

[
16
]  Philip denied the meeting with Ms. Govereau in mid-November, and denied giving her an unjustified hard time with respect to her work. He said that Ms. Govereau (unlike Ms. Janzen) was not a good waitress from the beginning, that there had been customer complaints, and that matters culminated with an incident on December 8, 1982, leading to her dismissal.

[
17
]  During the evening of December 8th, a Wednesday, Philip was acting as cook on the evening shift and Ms. Govereau was the sole waitress on duty. It was anticipated that there would not be many customers that evening, but Ms. Govereau says that as sole waitress she was very occupied. During the course of the evening an altercation developed between Ms. Govereau and some customers. One of the customers came to the kitchen to complaint to Philip about Ms. Govereau's rudeness, and Philip was obliged to come into the restaurant area and tend to that particular table of guests. At closing time Philip spoke with Ms. Govereau and told her that he was obliged to terminate her services, and he gave her two-weeks' notice. Philip contended (but his evidence on this point was rejected by the adjudicator) that only at this point in time did Ms. Govereau complain of previous sexual harassment on the part of Tommy the cook.

[
18
]  Ms. Govereau worked a further three days and then ended her employment with Platy.

[
19
]  The two complaints by Ms. Janzen and Ms. Govereau were processed under the machinery of
The Human Rights Act.
Mr. Yude Henteleff, Q.C. was appointed as adjudicator. He heard testimony from Ms. Janzen, Ms. Govereau, another waitress at the restaurant, and from Philip. Tommy Grammas was not available. He was not served with notice of the proceedings, and of course, he did not testify. He employment at Pharos Restaurant had long since ended.

[
20
]  The adjudicator wrote reasons for judgment extending for some 144 pages [reported
1985 CanLII 5235 (MB HRC)
,
6 C.H.R.R. D/2735
]. He held that both women had been sexually harassed by Tommy the cook. A monetary award under the
Act
was made against him in his absence. For Ms. Janzen the award was $480.00 lost wages, plus exemplary damages of $3,500.00. For Ms. Govereau the lost wages' award was $3,000.00 and the exemplary damages $3,000.00 as well.

[
21
]  Platy was found jointly and severally liable to the claimants for the same amounts. No award was made against Philip. The complaints were against Platy and Tommy Grammas, and because of a six-month limitation provision within the
Act
,
it is not too late to claim against Philip in his personal capacity.

[
22
]  The liability of the corporation was based upon a finding by the adjudicator that Tommy the cook was "part of the directing mind of the corporation", and hence the corporation is personally rather than vicariously responsible. But, in addition, as I understand his reasons, the adjudicator seemed to be saying that liability could be imposed against Platy on a vicarious basis as well. On p. 69 [at D/2753, para. 22546] of his reasons, the adjudicator states:

The clear intent of s. 6(1), in respect of areas of discrimination arising therefrom, is not only to make the employer liable for any acts of sexual harassment directly committed by such employer, but also makes him responsible for any such acts committed by a person in authority during the course of his employment.

[
23
]  An appeal was taken by Platy before Monnin J. of the Court of Queen's Bench (
1985 CanLII 3070 (MB QB)
,
7 C.H.R.R. D/3309
,
[1986] 2 W.W.R. 273
). It is an appeal based upon the record before the adjudicator. Monnin J. concluded that sexual harassment did constitute discrimination on the basis of sex within the terms of the
Act
.
He found that the corporation was not personally liable to the complainants; that Philip was not guilty of sexual harassment, nor did he condone Tommy's actions, and that Tommy the cook "might well not have been a directing mind" of the corporation. Nevertheless, he held that the corporation was vicariously responsible because Tommy was a servant of the corporation who was "in a position of authority over the staff", and that the corporation was "bound by his actions".

[
24
]  Concerning damages, Monnin J. reduced the award of exemplary damages for Ms. Janzen from $3,500.00 to $1,000.00. Concerning Ms. Govereau, he reduced the loss of wages claim from $3,000.00 down to $500.00, and reduced exemplary damages for her from $3,000.00 to $1,500.00.

[
25
]  A further appeal brings the matter before this court. Platy continues to argue that harassment is not discrimination and that the corporation should not be found vicariously liable for what Tommy the cook has done. In addition, as in the hearing before Monnin J., it is argued that the entire proceeding is invalid on the ground that the adjudicative process is
ultra vires
of
section 96
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
,
and that the function of the adjudicator is that of a federally appointed judge.

[
26
]  There is a cross-appeal by the complainants to restore the original awards in damages.

Is Sexual Harassment Discrimination on the Basis of Sex Under the Terms of The Human Rights Act of Manitoba?

[
27
]  I do not think so. A contrary opinion is expressed in not one but several decision of adjudicators and judges which equate the two. I think those decisions are wrong. The word "discriminate" is assigned three meanings in
The Shorter Oxford English Dictionary
(3rd ed.), the first and third of which might be applicable to the word as used in the
Act
:

1.    To make or constitute a difference in or between; to differentiate . . .

2.    To make a distinction.

[
28
]  In this
Act
discrimination is a violation of the law. The word "discriminate" used in a pejorative sense, means an unjustified differentiation or distinction.

[
29
]  But whether it is socially inappropriate, not all discrimination is contrary to law. The
Act
bars discrimination in certain spheres of human activity, but not all. If a man decides to hand out dollar bills on the street corner, he is entitled to give them to women rather than men, or to children rather than adults, because such discrimination on the basis of sex or age, happily, is not prohibited. But such conduct clearly constitutes discrimination.

[
30
]  Sexual harassment embraces an entirely different concept. The word "harass" is given several definitions in
The Shorter Oxford English Dictionary,
the most pertinent for our purposes being to harry, or to trouble or vex by repeated attacks. Sexual harassment involves vexing or troubling a person with respect to sexual matters, such as repeatedly touching or making suggestions, or threats.

[
31
]  Sexual harassment is not socially acceptable conduct. Depending on the nature of it, it might constitute a criminal offence or a civil wrong under the common law. But I cannot understand how it can be equated with sexual discrimination.

[
32
]  I suppose it is conceivable to conjure up a hypothetical situation where the two would merge into one. Suppose that an employer wants to hire men only, but in ostensible compliance with the
Act
he hires women as well as men. Having done so, he then decides to make working conditions so miserable for the women that they will resign. His tactic is to use sexual harassment to achieve his discriminatory purpose. Such a scenario may be conceivable, but it did not happen that way in the present case, and short of that sort of format, the two concepts do not coincide.

[
33
]  When a schoolboy steals kisses from a female classmate, one might well say that he is harassing her. He is troubling her; vexing her; harrying her;  but he surely is not discriminating against her.

[
34
]  Counsel for the Human Rights Commission argues that the complaints are under
section 6(1)
of the
Act
,
which relate to discrimination in respect of employment rather than discrimination at large. Quite so. But as a starting point, in order to impose liability and damages upon Tommy the cook or his employer, one must be able to say that harassment is included within the term discrimination. Save in the exceptional circumstances to which I have alluded, the argument falters and fails at this point.

[
35
]  I am conscious, of course, that it is within the power of a legislative body to say that black is white, or that day is night, or that harassment is discrimination. At least one legislative body, namely, the Parliament of Canada, has done so, but not Manitoba. Federal legislation now states that, "it is a discriminatory practice . . . in matters related to employment, to harass an individual on a prohibited ground of discrimination."

[
36
]  In other provinces such as Quebec, Newfoundland, and Ontario, without so torturing the Queen's English, human rights legislation has been amended by specifically providing that harassment on the basis of a prohibited ground such as sex will constitute a violation of the enactment, additional to the usual prohibitions on discrimination.

[
37
]  In Manitoba the key provision is
section 6(1)
of the
Act
which reads as follows:

6.(1)   Every person has the right of equality of opportunity based upon bona fide qualifications in respect of his occupation or employment or in respect of training for employment or in respect of an intended occupation, employment, advancement or promotion, and in respect of his membership or intended membership in a trade union, employers' organization or occupational association; and, without limiting the generality of the foregoing:

(a)   no employer or person acting on behalf of an employer, shall refuse to employ, or to continue to employ or to train the person for employment or to advance or promote that person, or discriminate against that person in respect of employment or any term or condition of employment;

(b)   no employment agency shall refuse to refer a person for employment, or for training for employment, and

(c)   no trade union, employers' organization or occupational association shall refuse membership to, expel, suspend or otherwise discriminate against that person; or negotiate, on behalf of that person, an agreement that would discriminate against him;

because of race, nationality, religion, colour, sex, age, marital status, physical or mental handicap, ethnic or national origin, or political beliefs or family status of that person.

[
38
]  The opening words of section 6(1) seem to aim at discrimination in the sense of a distinction, and seem to exclude the concept of harassment. There is, in those opening words, a declaration of equality in terms of membership in a trade union. Surely this means that no one should be excluded from the union because that person is a Hindu, or over sixty years of age, or a female. The question of sexual harassment is simply not germane to union membership save in the most bizarre hypothetical factual scenario.

[
39
]  The wording of clause (a) itself, in my opinion, continues the concept of discrimination as a distinction based upon a prohibited ground, and would therefore exclude sexual harassment. When clause (a) specifies that no employer shall refuse to employ a person on the basis of sex, it surely means that when considering an applicant for employment, that person is not to be rejected by reason of being male or female. I concede that it is possible to imagine an employer attempting to gain sexual favours in return for hiring an applicant, but I do not think the purpose of this section was to deal with that mischief. Sexual harassment usually extends over a period of time, whereas job applications are often processed without even meeting the applicant face to face, or after a single sort interview.

[
40
]  It is to be observed that clause (a) prohibits discrimination by "an employer or a person acting on behalf of an employer". This provision is perfectly understandable if discrimination on the grounds of sex is understood in a generic sense. It is the employer who has a policy which would exclude women from employment or promotion, or alternatively, the personnel manager to whom the employer has delegated the authority to hire or promote. But the provision makes no sense if sexual harassment is included as a feature of sexual discrimination. The employer of the personnel manager would be prohibited from engaging in sexual harassment, but other employees  like Tommy the cook  could do so with impunity because he is neither the employer nor acting on his behalf. There would be no violation of the
Act
and hence no order could be made against the very person who was responsible for the sexual harassment. If the legislature intended to deal with sexual harassment, they would surely do so in terms that would interdict such conduct by all persons in the work place.

[
41
]  Clause (a) goes on to prohibit discrimination with respect to any term or condition of employment. The term of employment could include an employee benefit plan where benefits or privileges are given to one class of employees and not others. That is the sense in which the word discrimination is being used in that section. It does not relate to sexual harassment. If one turns to
section 7(2)
of the
Act
one finds a specific section which allows a "distinction" on the basis of sex with respect to certain types of employee benefit plans.

[
42
]  It is also useful to consider clause (c) of
section 6(1)
which deals with trade unions, and which prohibits a trade union from negotiating a contract on behalf of a person which would discriminate against that person on the basis of race, nationality, religion, colour, sex, age, marital status, physical or mental handicap, ethnic or national origin, or political beliefs or family status. Clearly under clause (c) discrimination is used in the sense of differentiating or making a distinction. Clause (c) has nothing to do with sexual harassment.

[
43
]  Viewing the section as a whole, it is my conclusion that it is aimed at discrimination in a generic sense; blacks as a group, Jehovah's Witnesses as a group, or women as a group. That concept is also reflected in other provisions of the
Act
.

Section 6(1)
deals with discrimination in employment, but it is worthwhile to review other provisions in the
Act
which prohibit discrimination in other spheres of human conduct.
Section 2(1)
bars discrimination because of sex and other grounds, in terms of advertisements, notices or broadcasts. I think it is quite clear that the word discrimination as used in section 2(1) was never intended to include or relate to sexual harassment.

[
44
]
Section 3(1)
of the
Act
prohibits discrimination on the basis of sex, and other grounds, in relation to ". . . accommodation, service, facility, goods, right, licence or privilege available to the public or to a section of the public . . ." In simple terms, this section is aimed at those who would refuse to lease or sell to a person who is a member of a generic class such as a Jew or a black. Discrimination, as it is used in
section 3(1)
, does not seem to include the concept of sexual harassment.

[
45
]  Section 4(1) deals more specifically, but in a similar way, with housing accommodation. Interestingly, there are two exceptions to the ban on discrimination in terms of housing accommodation. An exception is made with respect to age to allow senior citizen housing projects. And an exception is made with respect to sex to permit, as an example, men's and women's dormitories at a university. Once again it is clear that the discrimination referred to in section 4 does not embrace sexual harassment.

[
46
]  Section 5 deals with the purchase of land or an interest in land, and once again it is clear that the word "discriminate" as used in that section was never intended to include sexual harassment.

[
47
]  In short, looking at the
Act
as a whole, the only reasonable conclusion is that sexual discrimination is something entirely different from, and does not include, sexual harassment.

[
48
]  In the hearing before the adjudicator, the question of whether sexual harassment constituted discrimination under the
Act
was not even raised or argued. In his lengthy written reasons there is but a single page dealing with this issue, which begins with this sentence [at D/2766, para. 22630]:

Let me also further state at this point that although this matter was not raised by either counsel, it is appropriate to state for the purpose of this judgment that subsection 6(1) of the
Human Rights Act,
supra, includes a prohibition against sexual harassment.

[
49
]  The adjudicator then went on to refer to a number of previous adjudications plus the decision of the Federal Court of Appeal in
Brennan
v.
Canada and Robichaud

(1985),
57 N.R. 116
,
1985 CanLII 5265 (FCA)
,
6 C.H.R.R. D/2695
(
sub. nom.
Treasury Board
v.
Robichaud
) in support of his conclusion.

[
50
]  By the time the matter was re-argued on appeal before Monnin J., there was a change of legal counsel for Platy, and the issue was vigorously argued on appeal. However, Monnin J. came to the same conclusion, referring and relying upon the decision of adjudicator O. B. Shime, Q.C. in
Bell and Korczak
v.
Ladas and The Flaming Steer Steak House

(1980),
1980 CanLII 3899 (ON HRT)
,
1 C.H.R.R. D/155
. Monnin J. noted that the decision of Mr. Shime in that case was the first dealing with sexual harassment under Ontario human rights legislation. That decision has subsequently been followed both by courts and boards of adjudication. When it was decided, the Ontario
Act
was framed much like the Manitoba
Act
of today, with a general prohibition against various kinds of discrimination in employment, but with no specific reference to sexual harassment. Mr. Shime's comments were
obiter
because he subsequently found that the evidence was not sufficiently reliable for him to find that a violation of the Code had taken place.
Obiter
or not, his words have influenced subsequent cases, and should be considered [at para. 1387]:

In my view the purpose of The Code is to establish uniform working conditions for employees and to remove those matters enumerated in Section 4 as relevant considerations in the work place. Consideration of matters such as ”˜race, creed, colour, age, sex, marital status, nationality or place of origin' strikes at what the preamble of The Code refers to ”˜the foundations of freedom, justice and peace', and infringes on the ”˜freedom and equality in dignity and rights' which this province and this society revere as commonly held values and have enshrined those in The Code. Thus, The Code prohibits these values from becoming negative factors in the employment relationship.

Subject to the exception provided in Section 4(6), discrimination based on sex is prohibited by The Code. Thus, the paying of a female person less than a male person for the same job is prohibited, or dismissing an employee on the basis of sex is also prohibited. But what about sexual harassment? Clearly a person who is disadvantaged because of her sex is being discriminated against in her employment when employer conduct denies her financial rewards because of her sex, or exacts some form of sexual compliance to improve or maintain her existing benefits.
The evil to be remedied is the utilization of economic power or authority so as to restrict a woman's guaranteed and equal access to the workplace and all its benefits, free from extraneous pressures having to do with the mere fact that she is a woman.
Where a woman's equal access is denied or where terms and conditions differ when compared to male employees, the woman is being discriminated against.

The forms of prohibited conduct that, in my view, are discriminatory run the gamut from overt gender based activity, such as coerced intercourse to unsolicited physical contact to persistent propositions to more subtle conduct such as gender based insults and taunting, which may reasonably be perceived to create a negative psychological and emotional work environment. There is no reason why the law, which reaches into the workplace so as to protect the work environment from physical or chemical pollution or extremes of temperature, ought not to protect employees as well from negative, psychological and mental effects where adverse and gender directed conduct emanating from a management hierarchy may reasonably be construed to be a condition of employment.

[
51
]  It is easy to agree with the sentiments expressed in these paragraphs, and indeed, much of what has been written by Mr. Shime is valid with respect to section 6(1) of the Manitoba legislation. However, in my opinion, the evil which the
Act
was intended to remedy is discrimination on a generic basis, which does not include sexual harassment. Mr. Shime is correct in equating sexual harassment with the abuse of economic power or authority. If the
Act
was intended to prohibit such conduct, it should have so specified because such conduct is not included within the ambit of discrimination.

[
52
]  It is true that, as Mr. Shime suggests, there is no reason why statutory law controlling the work environment cannot prohibit the abuse of economic power in the form of sexual harassment. But the words of the statute must make it clear that such a reach was intended. The Manitoba
Act,
as I have pointed out, is not a piece of labour legislation dealing with safety in the work place, but rather legislation which deals with advertising, accommodation, and a broad range of other contractual relationships, as well as employment. The focus of the
Act
is not on the work place, but upon this wide range of human relationships where discrimination — but not sexual harassment — is to be precluded.

[
53
]  Many cases have been decided, subsequent to the
Bell and Korczak
decision,
supra,
which specifically agreed with Mr. Shime's assessment of the law, or proceeded on the assumption that sexual harassment did constitute discrimination on the basis of sex. This is surprising, not just because the decision is, on its face, a questionable interpretation of the words in the Ontario statute, but because it was preceded in time by a judgment of the Superior Court which points in an opposite direction. Johnson J. of the Saskatchewan Court of Queen's Bench wrote the judgment in
Re Board of Governors of the University of Saskatchewan et al. and Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission

(1976),
1976 CanLII 1252 (SK QB)
,
66 D.L.R. (3d) 561
. The issue in that case was different. The university had ruled that a sessional lecturer would not be allowed to supervise practice teaching in public schools because he was a homosexual. The Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission embarked upon an inquiry. The university moved for and obtained an order of prohibition from Johnson J. In his reasons for judgment, Johnson J. deals with section 3 of the
Fair Employment Practices Act,

R.S.S. 1965, c. 293
(as amended in 1972), which states that "No employer shall . . . discriminate against any person in regard to employment or any term or condition of employment because of . . . sex." He held that sex, as used in section 3 relates to the male or female gender, and not the sexual practices of a particular person:

In the
Fair Employment Practices Act,
the provision for prohibiting employment discrimination against any person on the basis of his sex would generally be considered to be on the basis of whether or not that person was a man or woman, not on his sexual orientation, his sexual proclivity, or sexual activity. In other words, sex as used in s. 3 would generally and popularly be regarded as referring to the gender of the employee or prospective employee and not to the sexual activities or propensities of that person. It should be noted that the section in question prohibits discrimination on the basis of his race, his religion, his sex, etc., and not on the basis of his sexual activities, his sexual propensity or his sexual orientation.

]  With respect, I think it is a mistake to rely upon the opening sentence of the section to justify the conclusion that sexual harassment is prohibited. The whole thrust of the section, and indeed the

,

.
(1985),

,
19 D.L.R. (4th) 148
, 6 C.H.R.R. D/2861 was decided by the Nova Scotia Supreme Court, Appeal Division, with reasons by Jones J. A. He was dealing with the Nova Scotia

Discrimination and the Law in Canada

Since that text was written there have been a number of board decisions in Canada following the decision of Chairman Shime in the case of

1980 CanLII 3899 (ON HRT)
,
27 L.A.C. (2d) 227
,

,006. For a more recent review of the cases

McPherson

”˜Mary's Donuts' and Hachik Doshoian,

1982 CanLII 4873 (ON HRT)
,
3 C.H.R.R. D/961

[
63
]  I can only say that unlike the Tarnopolsky text, I do not think that Mr. Shime's decision ". . . provides an excellent guide as to how the law should be applied in Canada." I do not think that the subsequent decisions of adjudicators in various jurisdictions have made the case any stronger. I am not impressed with recent American authorities representing as they do a complete volte-face in the development of the jurisprudence on this subject in the United States. I remain convinced that the sort of sexual discrimination involved in this case does not constitute discrimination under the Manitoba
Act,
and is not a violation of the
