,
and consequently, in spite of the list of decisions marshalled on behalf of the complainants, the complaints must be dismissed.

[
64
]  While it may be unnecessary to deal with the other points at issue in the appeal, I propose to continue to review the question of the liability of the corporation, Platy, and the question as to whether the board of adjudication is a valid mechanism, under the
Constitution
for deciding such a case.

Liability of the Corporation:

[
65
]  In terms of discrimination in employment, clause (a) of
section 6(1)
of the
Act
speaks of the "employer or a person acting on behalf of an employer". In this case the employer, Platy, a corporate entity, was not involved in any discriminatory acts. The corporation had no policy of discrimination. There was no evidence that the corporation condoned the conduct of Tommy the cook.

[
66
]  The adjudicator imposed liability upon Tommy the cook. He was not the employer of the complainant. I do not see how it could be argued that he was "acting on behalf" of the corporation when he engaged in his strange amorous pursuits. If Tommy the cook was neither the employer, nor a person acting on behalf of the employer, then I am at a loss to understand how an order can be made against him, even if he were guilty of discriminatory conduct: His discriminatory conduct would not be prohibited by the
Act
.

[
67
]  The
Act
appears to be aimed at employers and those who implement the employers' discriminatory policy, rather than some co-employee who has been guilty of misconduct. It is Platy that is at risk in these proceedings.

[
68
]  At common law liability can be imposed upon a company for the
torts
of its servants who are acting within the course of their employment. Since discrimination is a newly-created statutory wrong, (at least when it is of a form other than sexual harassment), careful consideration is necessary before vicarious liability is to be imposed in relation to a violation of the
Act
.
In
Re Nelson et al. and Byron Price & Associates Ltd.

(1981),
1981 CanLII 415 (BC CA)
,
122 D.L.R. (3d) 340
, the British Columbia Court of Appeal indicated the authority to impose vicarious liability must be found within the legislation, otherwise vicarious responsibility cannot be imposed. That case dealt with discrimination in housing where the employee of a rental agent was guilty of discriminatory conduct and where the issue before the court was whether liability could be imposed vicariously upon her employer. Craig J. A., for a unanimous court, stated at 346:

I have no doubt that the legislation is remedial and that in accordance with s. 8 of our
Interpretation Act,
R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 206, it should be given such ”˜fair, large and liberal interpretation as best ensures the attainment of its objects', but I have no doubt, also, that in striving for this interpretation a Court should not ascribe a meaning to words in the legislation which would normally be inconsistent with the grammatical and ordinary sense of the words used in the
Act
as a whole. I think that there is much to be said for the view that an employer should bear responsibility, in some form, for discriminatory conduct of an employee in the course of his employment but that is a decision for the Legislature, not for a Court. Our sole concern is whether s. 17 of the
Human Rights Code
provides for vicarious liability. The operative phrase throughout s. 17 is ”˜person who contravened this Act'. In this case, the only conclusion is that the board found that the respondent did not contravene the Act. Notwithstanding this finding, the board concluded that the respondent was ”˜vicariously liable' for the contraventions by Mrs. Gubbins. While this result maybe desirable, it cannot, in my opinion, be inferred from the legislation. To find the respondent ”˜vicariously liable' would require reading words into the statute which are, in my opinion, not justified.

[
69
]  The
Nelson
case,
supra,
was followed in the decision of the majority in the Federal Court of Appeal in
Brennan
v.
Canada and Robichaud, supra.
In that case the complainant, Bonnie Robichaud, alleged that Mr. Brennan had discriminated against her by sexually harassing her. Mrs. Robichaud was a member of the cleaning staff of a military establishment and Mr. Brennan was her supervisor. The Federal Court of Appeal dealt with the question of whether Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth might be held vicariously responsible for Mr. Brennan's inappropriate sexual aggression. Not surprisingly, it was decided that Queen Elizabeth was not responsible; that there was no basis in law for imposing strict liability upon an employer for the discriminatory acts of an employee, and that it would take a clear statutory directive to create vicarious responsibility. Thurlow C. J. stated at 132 [D/2703 at para. 22278 of C.H.R.R.]:

. . . I see nothing in the . . . statute to say that a person is to be held vicariously or absolutely or strictly liable in accordance with common law tort or criminal law principles for discrimination engaged in by someone else, whether an employee or not.

[
70
]  In the present case the adjudicator concluded that the
Brennan
v.
Canada and
Robichaud
case,
supra,
was not applicable because it dealt with Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth rather than an ordinary employer. With respect, I think the principle expressed by Thurlow C. J. is applicable to all employers.

[
71
]  In my opinion, the approach taken by Craig J. A.
in the
Nelson
case,
supra,
and Thurlow C. J. in the
Brennan
case,
supra,
makes good sense. If this sort of liability is to be imposed, it is not too much to expect that the statute will so specify in clear terms.

[
72
]  It is to be noted that
The Human Rights Act
of Manitoba, under section 28(2)(c) authorizes the board of adjudication to impose "a penalty or exemplary damages." It makes little sense to impose liability in terms of a penalty or punitive damages against one who has been guilty of no fault and is deserving of no punishment. The imposition of punishment against one who deserves no punishment is so manifestly unjust that it would require a specific statutory foundation.

[
73
]  Looking at the various provisions of the
Act
,
it is my opinion that no such foundation exists in the Manitoba legislation.

[
74
]
Section 6(1)
of the
Act
states that "no employer or person acting on behalf of an employer", shall discriminate against a person interms of employment. If the employer is directly involved in the discriminatory conduct, then the employer is to be held responsible. So is an employee who is acting on behalf of an employer. But there is no suggestion or implication that the employer is to be held responsible for the discriminatory conduct of an employee who is not "acting on behalf of an employer". However one might describe the conduct of Tommy the cook in this case, there can be no dispute that he was not "acting on behalf of an employer".

[
75
]  Section 6(1), once again, must be considered in conjunction with section 28(2) which delineates the powers of a board of adjudication. Section 28(2) reads as follows:

28.(2)  Where the board of adjudication decides that a party has contravened any provision of the
Act
, it may do one or more of the following things:

(a)   Make an order requiring the party who contravened the
Act
to do or refrain from doing anything in order to secure compliance wiht the Act.

(b)   Make an order requiring the party who contravened the
Act
to compensate the person discriminated against for all, or such part as a board may determine, of any wages or salary lost or expenses incurred by reason of the contravention of this Act.

(c)   Order the person who contravened the
Act
to pay to the person discriminated against, a penalty or exemplary damages in such amount as the board may determine, if the board is of the opinion that the person discriminated against suffered damages in respect of his feelings, or self-respect.

[
76
]  There is no authority under section 28(2) to make an order other than against "the party" or "the person who has contravened the
Act
". The wording is similar to that which was
considered in the
Nelson
case,
supra,
and the
Brennan
case,
supra.
Far from providing that vicarious liability might be imposed, the
Act
seems to say precisely the opposite.

[
77
]  In
Dakota Ojibway Tribal Council
v.
Bewza

(1985),
1985 CanLII 3129 (MB CA)
,
37 Man. R. (2d) 207
, this court considered section 28(2) in the context of an alleged claim of racial discrimination with respect to accommodation. Twaddle J. A. considered the meaning of the words "party" as defined by the
Act
,
and "person" as defined by the
Act
and as defined by
The Interpretation Act,
C.C.S.M. c. I80. He concluded that with respect to that form of discrimination the liability under the
Act
was personal rather than vicarious:

Notwithstanding, the personal nature of an act of discrimination is such that in my view it cannot amount to a contravention of the
Act
by anyone other than the discriminator unless a partnership or corporate policy to discriminate can be established or the partnership or corporation is shown to be an accomplice to the act of discrimination.

[
78
]  In my opinion, the decision in
Dakota Ojibway Tribal Council
v.
Bewza
, supra,
is applicable
to the present case.

[
79
]  Finally, I must observe that even if the statute did contemplate vicarious liability, it could only arise if the employee was acting within the terms of his actual, implied or ostensible authority, and that the act complained of occurred in the course of employment. There was no authority, express or implied, for Tommy the cook to sexually harass waitresses. I do not intend to pause to consider the question at length, but I see no basis to support a suggestion that he had ostensible authority to do so. Further, I do not think that his unseemly activities were performed "during the course of his employment". Patting the buttocks of a waitress is
dehors
his job as a cook. This point will be explored more thoroughly in these reasons when the issue of personal liability on Platy is considered.

[
80
]  The adjudicator imposed liability upon Platy on a second ground, namely that Tommy the cook was the "operating mind" of the corporation, and consequently his acts constituted the acts of the corporation itself, and thus Platy becomes personally rather than vicariously responsible. On this basis it can be argued that Platy itself contravened the
Act
,
based on what has become known as the organic theory of corporate responsibilty.

[
81
]  Where a corporation adopts or approves the wrongful acts of its servant, then those acts become the act of the corporation itself. Similarly, where the corporation puts one of its officers or officials in a position where he is free to originate the corporation's policies and implement them, then the acts of the officer or official become the acts of the corporation. Where, for example, a company authorizes its managing director to establish his own criteria for hiring new employees without supervision or interference, and he proceeds to discriminate on a prohibited ground, the corporation is itself guilty of a violation of the
Act
.
In this important sphere of employment the managing director has become the operating or directing mind of the corporation.

[
82
]  The organic theory is exemplified by the leading case of
Lennards' Carrying Company Limited
v.
Asiatic Petroleum Company Limited,

[1915] A.C. 705
. A corporation owned a ship which was unseaworthy. By virtue of a provision in the British
Merchant Shipping Act,
1894, the owner of the ship was not to be held liable for any loss or damage happening without his actual fault. Mr. Lennard, the managing director of the corporation, was the individual who was aware that the ship was unseaworthy, and failed to take steps to prevent it from going to sea in that condition, andconsequently a loss occurred. The House of Lords, in a judgment by Viscount Haldane, L. C., concluded that there was "actual fault" on the part of the corporation, because the managing director was the directing mind of the corporation, and hence his acts or omissions became the acts of omissions of the corporation itself. Viscount Haldane L. C. wrote at 713:

My Lords, a corporation is an abstraction. It has no mind of its own any more than it has a body of its own; its active and directing will must consequently be sought in the person of somebody who for some purposes may be called an agent, but who is really the directing mind and will of the corporation, the very ego and centre of the personality of the corporation.

[
83
]  Viscount Haldane L. C. went on to say that in the absence of testimony from Mr. Lennard to the contrary, it was open to the court to conclude that he was "the life and soul of the company" or "the directing mind of the company".

[
84
]  In
R.
v.
St. Lawrence Corp. Ltd. et al.,

1969 CanLII 504 (ON CA)
,
[1969] 2 O.R. 305
, the Ontario Court of Appeal held that a large corporation might have separate directing or operating minds in its various divisions or branch offices.

[
85
]  In his text,
Vicarious Liability in the Law of Torts
(1967), P. S. Atiyah suggests the distinction between vicarious liabilty and personal liability, based on the "directing mind" concept, has little importance in the law of tort. In both cases the liability will be imposed if the employee — whether the operating mind of the corporation or not — is acting within his authority or ostensible authority, and is in the course of his employment. But like the
Lennard's
case,
supra,
itself, the distinction is an important one in a case such as the present one where no foundation for imposing vicarious liability is established in the legislation.

[
86
]  The organic theory of corporate responsibility has been applied in other human rights cases: the two decisions by Professor P. A. Cumming in
Iancu
v.
Simcoe County Board of Education

(1983),
1983 CanLII 4720 (ON HRT)
,
4 C.H.R.R. D/1203
, and
Olarte et al.
v.
DeFilippis and Commodore Business Machines Ltd., supra,
being prime examples. In my opinion, it is appropriate that the organic theory of corporate responsibility be applied to human rights cases, where the facts justify the application of the theory.

[
87
]  In this particular case, I do not think the organic theory supports the imposition of liability for two reasons; firstly, because Tommy the cook was not the directing mind of the corporation; and secondly, because the alleged acts of discrimination were not committed "in the course of employment".

[
88
]  Tommy Grammas was not an officer nor a director of Platy, nor a person in a senior management position. He was the cook, paid on an hourly basis, working the evening shift. He exercised no managerial responsibilities except that, on slow nights, he would decide which waitress or waitresses would be released before the end of the shift. He had no authority to discipline fellow employees, and there is no evidence that he ever attempted to exercise that authority. He did not have the right to hire or fire, and again, there is no evidence that he pretended to that authority, although Philip does concede that for disciplinary purposes the waitressing staff were left with the impression that he did have that power. But this is hardly the stuff that makes, to use Lord Haldane's words, ". . . the directing mind and will of the corporation, the very ego and centre of the personality of the corporation."

[
89
]  In the text
Vicarious Liability in the Law of Torts, supra,
P. S. Atiyah writes of the difficulty in determining who is to be considered a directing mind of a corporate entity:

The subsequent development of this form of liability belongs largely to the criminal law for it is only in that branch of the law that the distinction between personal and vicarious liability generally has any practical significance. The cases on criminal liability show that there is often serious difficulty in deciding whether the acts of a particular servant of the company are to be treated as the acts of the company itself, but the most recent cases show a tendency to restrict this concept to those servants who may be said to be ”˜the brains' of the company, such as directors, managers and other ”˜responsible officers'.

[
90
]  It is simply overreaching to suggest that Tommy the cook was the "brains" of the company, or its directing mind. In my opinion Monnin J. was right in observing that Tommy the cook "might well not have been a directing mind" of Platy. Monnin J. could have stated the matter in stronger terms without error.

[
91
]  Moreover, Tommy the cook was not in the course of his employment when he sexually harassed the two co-employees. A master is liable for the acts of his negligent employee when the negligent act is simply a way of performing what the employee is authorized and expected to do. If the cook dumped too much pepper in the soup, he would clearly be acting in the course of his employment, trying, albeit negligently, to prepare and present a decent meal. If the cook, contrary to instruction, was smoking on the job, and as a result caused a gas explosion in the kitchen, it would be arguable that he was still acting in the course of his employment in the sense that he was trying to fulfill his responsibilities as a cook. But what has patting the buttocks of a waitress to do with fulfilling the responsibilities as a cook? In his text, P. S. Atiyah comments on wilful acts, and the question of whether they are in the course of employment. He suggests the proper test for imposing liability on the master is this:

. . . is the servant's tort an act of a kind sufficiently similar to the acts he has been authorised to perform?; is there a substantial risk that the employer's object cannot be achieved without torts of this kind being committed by his servants?

[
92
]  It is easy to answer these questions in the present case. The acts complained of, constituting sexual harassment, are in no way similar to what Tommy Grammas was authorized to do. There is no substantial risk that a cook is likely to sexually harass other staff members while making the soup.

[
93
]  I return briefly to the first issue in dispute on this appeal, namely, whether sexual harassment constitutes discrimination. Where a company authorizes a managing director to hire new employees without direction or supervison, there is indeed a substantial risk that discrimination on a prohibited ground is apt to take place. It makes sense that the organic theory of corporate responsibiltiy would apply to discrimination in those terms, but not where the nature of the discrimination is sexual harassment.

[
94
]  Some comment with respect to Philip is necessary. The complaints do not specifically mention Philip. The complaints are directed against Tommy Grammas and Platy and "its owners, agents and servants". But Philip was a director of the company, and the manager of the St. Vital restaurant, and in terms of that operation, he was indeed the directing mind of the corporation.

[
95
]  The adjudicator was highly critical of Philip. He found that Philip was not a credible witness. He concluded that Philip was unsympathetic to the complainants and took no action in response to their complaints. He found Philip to be responsible for poisoning the atmosphere to the point that Ms. Janzen resigned under circumstances which the adjudicator considered a constructive dismissal. Concerning Ms. Govereau, the adjudicator concluded that Philip had joined with Tommy the cook in unjustified criticisms of Ms. Govereau's abilities as a waitress, and that the giving of notice to Ms. Govereau to terminate her services was "unjustified". I join with Monnin J. who, on the initial appeal, said this of Philip's conduct [at D/3314, para. 24637, of C.H.R.R.]:

At the outset, although I find that respondents' officer, Philip Anastasiadis, might not have been the most understanding and the most responsive employer to the complaints of his employees, I do not accept that his conduct per se amounted to sexual harassment. Neither do I find that respondents at any time condoned Grammas' actions.

[
96
]  Like Monnin J. I am mindful of the respect that is to be accorded to the findings of fact made by the initial trier of facts. But in my opinion, some of the criticisms of Philip simply go too far. At one point, for example, the adjudicator implies that Philip's testimony is less than reliable because Philip chose not to call Tommy Grammas as a witness to corroborate a particular point in his testimony. But in fact, Tommy Grammas' employment had been terminated, and not even the Human Rights Commission was able to find him in order to notify him of the complaints or of the hearing itself.

[
97
]  If one accepts the evidence of Ms. Janzen in its entirety, then it is clear that when the complaint of sexual harassment was made Philip was less understanding and sympathetic than he should have been, although there is no question that he offered Ms. Janzen employment in one of Platy's other restaurants where she would feel more comfortable. It is also uncontradicted that sexual harassment of Ms. Janzen had stopped by the time she made her complaint to Philip.

[
98
]  If one accepts the evidence of Ms. Govereau in its entirety, then again, the sexual harassment by Tommy the cook ended as soon as a complaint was made to Philip. Ms. Govereau contends that another form of harassment relating to her work then began, and that Philip joined with Tommy the cook in making life difficult for her. It is entirely possible that, having been rebuffed, Tommy Grammas did make life unpleasant for Ms. Govereau. Not having been rebuffed himself, I cannot understand why Philip would suddenly join in a conspiracy against Ms. Govereau. It is to be remembered that so long as it did not related to a prohibited ground of discrimination, Philip (or Platy) was entitled to terminate the services of Ms. Govereau at any time, without cause, upon giving her reasonable notice, or pay in lieu of notice. That is eventually what Philip did, but at the same time, Philip contends that he did have cause for dismissal. The evidence is abundantly clear that there was a precipitating event to his giving notice to Ms. Govereau which might well have justified termination without notice. While I can appreciate the difficulties of a waitress trying to keep customers happy during a hectic time, I can also appreciate that a restaurant owner cannot tolerate a waitress who is argumentative and rude with customers.

[
99
]  There is no evidence that Philip discriminated against either of the two complainants on any prohibited ground (even if sexual harassment is included within the ambit of discrimination on the grounds of sex). The necessary prerequisites for an order against Philip or, through Philip against Platy, under section 28(2)(b) and (c), covering wages, expenses, and exemplary damages, is therefore missing.

[
100
]  In order to succeed the complainants must establish that what Tommy the cook did constitutes discrimination, and that Platy is liable for his actions. In my opinion, the complainants fail on both counts.

Constitutional Issue:

[
101
]  Platy raises a third ground of appeal; namely, that the board of adjudication is
ultra vires

section 96
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
.
I agree with Monnin J. that the process, insofar as it relates to discrimination and not sexual harassment, does not violate the
Constitution Act.

[
102
]  The leading case if
Reference Re Residential Tenancies Act

(1981),
1981 CanLII 24 (SCC)
,
123 D.L.R. (3d) 554
, a judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada written by Dickson J. That case sets forth a three-step test to determine whether a provincially-appointed board, such as a board of adjudication under the
Act
,
transgresses the power of the federal government to appoint judges to determine causes under section 96. The three-step test is set forth in these terms at 571–572:

The first involves consideration, in the light of the historical conditions existing in 1867, of the particular power or jurisdiction conferred upon the tribunal. The question here is whether the power or jurisdiction conforms to the power or jurisdiction exercised by Superior, District or County Courts at the time of Confederation. This temporary segregation, or isolation, of the impugned power is not for the purpose of turning back the clock and restoring
Toronto
v.
York
as the governing authority, an approach deplored in
Mississauga.
It is rather the first step in a three step process.

If the historical inquiry leads to the concluson that the power or jurisdiction is not broadly conformable to jurisdiction formerly exercised by s. 96 Courts, that is the end of the matter. As Rand J. noted in
A. E. Dupont et al.
v.
Inglis et al.

(1958),
1958 CanLII 8 (SCC)
,
14 D.L.R. (2d) 417
at p. 424,
[1958] S.C.R. 535
at p. 542
: ”˜Judicial power, not of that type [
i.e.,
that exercised by s. 96 Courts at Confederation], such as that exercised by inferior Courts, can be conferred on a Provincial tribunal whatever its primary character.' If, however, the historical evidence indicates that the impugned power is identical or analogous to a power exercised by s. 96 Courts at Confederation, then one must proceed to the second step of the inquiry.

Step two involves consideration of the function within its institutional setting to determine whether the function itself is different when viewed in that setting. In particular, can the function still be considered to be a ”˜judicial' function? In addressing the issue, it is important to keep in mind the further statement by Rand J. in
Dupont
v.
Inglis
[at p. 424 D.L.R., p. 543 S.C.R.] that ”˜it is the subject-matter rather than the apparatus of adjudication that is determinative'. Thus the question of whether any particular function is ”˜judicial' is not to be determined simply on the basis of procedural trappings. The primary issue is the nature of the question which the tribunal is called upon to decide. Where the tribunal is faced with a private dispute between parties, and is called upon to adjudicate through the application of a recognized body of rules in a manner consistent with fairness and impartiality, then, normally, it is acting in a ”˜judicial capacity'. To borrow the terminology of Professor Ronald Dworkin, the judicial task involves questions of ”˜principle', that is, consideration of the competing rights of individuals or groups. This can be contrasted with questions of ”˜policy' involving competing views of the collective good of the community as a whole: see Dworkin,
Taking Rights Seriously
(1977), at pp. 82–90 (Duckworth).

If, after examining the institutional context, it becomes apparent that the power is not being exercised as a ”˜judicial power' then the inquiry need go no further for the power, within its institutional context, no longer conforms to a power or jurisdiction exercisable by a s. 96 Court and the provincial scheme is valid. On the other hand, if the power or jurisdiction is exercised in a judicial manner, then it becomes necessary to proceed to the third and final step in the analysis and review the tribunal's function as a whole in order to appraise the impugned function in its entire institutional context. The phrase — ”˜it is not the detached jurisdiction or power alone that is to be considered but rather its setting in the institutional arrangements in which it appears' — is the central core of the judgment in
Tomko.
It is no longer sufficient simply to examine the particular power or function of a tribunal and ask whether this power or function was once exercised by s. 96 Courts. This would be examining the power or function in a ”˜detached' manner, contrary to the reasoning in
Tomko.
What must be considered is the ”˜context' in which this power is exercised.
Tomko
leads to the following result: it is possible for administrative tribunals to exercise powers and jurisdiction which once were exercised by the s. 96 Courts. It will all depend on the context of the exercise of the power. It may be that the impugned ”˜judicial powers' are merely subsidiary or ancillary to general administrative functions assigned to the tribunal
(John East, Tomko)
or the powers may be necessarily incidental to the achievement of a broader policy goal for the Legislature
(Mississauga).
In such a situation, the grant of judicial power to provincial appointees is valid. The scheme is only invalid when the adjudicative function is a sole or central function of the tribunal
(Farrah)
so that the tribunal can be said to be operating ”˜like a s. 96 Court'.

[
103
]  My agreement with the conclusion of Monnin J. is based upon the earlier view which I have expressed that discrimination on the basis of sex does not include sexual harassment. At the time of Confederation, an employer was entitled to discriminate on the basis of race, age, sex, and so forth. Human rights legislation, across the country, has created entirely new concepts and it is appropriate that boards of adjudication be established to adjudicate disputes in this new area.

[
104
]  But to the extent that sexual harassment is included in the concept of discrimination on the basis of sex, then I would hold a contrary view. Sexual harassment, in terms of unwanted touching and kissing of the type involved in this case, constitutes an assault, which was a matter with which the civil and criminal courts of 1867 were fully equipped to deal. It is true that sexual harassment might take a form somewhat different than an assault, such as verbal abuse, taunts or threats, but in whatever form, it will be "analogous to" the kind of offence which was determinable by s. 96 Courts at the time of Confederation.

[
105
]  I am mindful that the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal
in
Re Mehta and MacKinnon
et al., supra,
concluded that a board of adjudication dealing with a sexual harassment case "does not encompass a function exercised by a superior court at the time of Confederation".

[
106
]  The report of the case does not indicate the nature of the sexual harassment which was alleged. Perhaps it was of a nature that took it outside of the category of analogous to an assault.

[
107
]  If one were to proceed to the second step of the test, I think there is no doubt that the proceeding before the board of adjudication is judicial in nature. The question to be decided is whether there has been a violation of the law by the respondents, in which case appropriate damages are to be assessed. The decision of the adjudicator becomes a judgment of the Court of Queen's Bench for enforcement purposes. I do not see that the lack of a privity clause has any significant bearing on the nature of the proceeding. After all, there are appeals from trial courts, but those proceedings are judicial in nature.

[
108
]  In
Re Scowby et al. and Glendinning

(1983),
1983 CanLII 2065 (SK CA)
,
148 D.L.R. (3d) 55
,
1983 CanLII 4731 (SK CA)
,
4 C.H.R.R. D/1355
, the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal concluded that a board of inquiry under the
Saskatchewan Human Rights Code,
S.S. 1979, c. S-24.1, to investigate a complaint of arbitrary arrest and detention did not violate s. 96 of the
Constitution Act
because the second and third steps of the test required a negative answer. The
Scowby
case was subsequently appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada and a decision was rendered on October 9, 1986 [reported
1986 CanLII 30 (SCC)
,
8 C.H.R.R. D/3677
]. The majority reasons for judgment, by Estey J. allow the appeal on the ground that the subject of arbitrary arrest and detention is under the exclusive jurisdiction of the government of Canada to legislate in the field of criminal law. There are minority reasons which agree with the judgment of Tallis J. A. of the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal, but with respect, I do not find those minority reasons convincing.

[
109
]  Both the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal and the minority of judges in the Supreme Court of Canada concluded that the function of the Human Rights Commission was not judicial because the
Code
has educational and social policy objectives which are intertwined with the decision-making functions of a board of inquiry. With respect, we are concerned here with the constitutional validity of the board of adjudication proceedings, not with other phases of the legislation. Whatever the functions of the Manitoba Human Rights Commission, the function of the adjudicator is to determine whether a violation of the
Act
has taken place, and if so, to make an appropriate order including the imposition of damages. The adjudicator's role is neither conciliatory nor educational.

[
110
]  With respect to the third test, I think it is clear from the
Act
that the board of adjudication has but a single, central function, namely to make a judicial determination and hence it can be said to operate like a section 96 Court.

[
111
]  In short, a board of adjudication established for the purpose of determining whether a case of sexual harassment has been established would be in contravention of
section 96
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
.
Since the Manitoba
Act
does not include a prohibition against sexual harassment, the legislation does not offend the constitutional requirements.

Damages:

[
112
]  There is a cross-appeal by the complainants to restore the award of exemplary damages as determined by the adjudicator.

[
113
]  In my opinion, Monnin J. was quite right in reducing the awards under section 28(2)(c).
The case of
Dakota Ojibway Tribal Council
v.
Bewza
, supra,
contains some useful comments on the subject of assessment of exemplary damages under the
Act
.
In my opinion, the award of Monnin J. is in keeping with those comments.

[
114
]  In summary, I would allow the appeal of Platy with costs in this court, together with a factum fee of $100.00. Platy is also entitled to costs on the hearing before Monnin J. in the Court of Queen's Bench, and costs on the hearing before the adjudicator.

Twaddle J. A.:

[
115
]  The primary issue on this appeal is whether or not sexual harassment is, or is capable of being, discrimination because of sex. On an appeal to the Court of Queen's Bench from a board of adjudication ("the board"), appointed under
The
Human Rights Act
,

C.C.S.M. c. H175
("the
Act
"), Monnin J. held that sexual harassment was discrimination and confirmed an award of compensation against the employer, Platy Enterprises Ltd. ("Platy"). From his decision, Platy now appeals.

[
116
]  Platy also appeals the finding that it was within the jurisdiction of the legislature to confer on a board of adjudication, constituted pursuant to a provincial
Act
,
the power to award compensation for the wrong of discrimination. The complainants, in turn, cross-appeal from the order of Monnin J. reducing the quantum of damages payable to them and from his ruling that the board had no jurisdiction to order Platy to establish in its places of employment a programme which would assure that such places remain free of sexual harassment.

[
117
]  I have had the opportunity of reading the reasons of my brother Huband for his judgment. The facts relevant to this appeal are set out fully in them and need not be repeated by me.

[
118
]  The initial question to be considered is whether or not in this case the victims of harassment were discriminated against contrary to
section 6(1)
of the
Act
,
the relevant part of which reads:

6.(1)   Every person has the right of equality of opportunity based upon bona fide qualifications in respect of his occupation or employment . . .; and, without limiting the generality of the foregoing

(a)   no employer or person acting on behalf of an employer, shall refuse to employ, or to continue to employ . . . the person . . . or discriminate against that person in respect of employment or any term of condition of employment;

. . .

because of race, nationality, religion, colour, sex, age, marital status, physical or mental handicap, ethnic or national origin, or political beliefs or family status of that person.

[
119
]  There are three elements of the wrong alleged:

(i)  discrimination;

(ii)  because of sex;

(iii)  in respect of employment.

Although I will consider each of these elements separately, I am of the view that their presence in any case cannot be assessed independently. They interrelate. Prohibited discrimination is not the sum of its elements, but is a composite resulting from a combination of conduct, cause and employment circumstances.

Discrimination

[
120
]  "Discriminate" is "to make or constitute a difference in or between":
The Oxford Universal Dictionary on Historical Principles
(3rd ed.). In this sense it is possible to discriminate between women with work experience and those without and between university graduates and school drop-outs. It is not, however, the differentiation between people because of individual qualifications that constitutes discrimination forbidden by the
Act
,
but differentiation between them because of categorical grouping. The
Act
requires that in respect of employment people be treated on the basis of individual merit and not because of a category to which they belong, a category irrelevant to qualification for employment. In this latter sense "discriminate" is defined by
Webster's Third New International Dictionary
as "to make a difference in treatment or favour on a class or categorical basis in disregard of individual merit." It is in this sense that the verb is most often used with the preposition "against", as it is in the
Act.

[
121
]  The intent of the legislature to confine discrimination to differentiation by category is confirmed by the list of forbidden reasons for discrimination. Most of the reasons are descriptive of a distinguishing feature which everyone has, but which differs between people. Thus, everyone has a nationality, a colour and a sex, but not everyone has the same nationality, colour or sex. Different people have different religious and political beliefs and even those without belief may themselves make up a category. The handicapped are in a category by themselves, but are to be protected from discrimination because of that. The legislature has directed its prohibition at distinguishing people by category, a distinction which results in people being dealt with on account of group characteristics, unrelated to merit, rather than individual ability and qualifications.

[
122
]  Discrimination in respect of employment can occur, as Professor Tarnopolsky (now Tarnopolsky J. A.) suggests in his text:
Discrimination and the Law
at p. 275, in one of three ways:

1.  evil motive or intent;

2.  differential treatment;

3.  disparate consequences or effects of a seemingly neutral practice.

The second and third of those ways were discussed by McIntyre J., delivering the judgment of the Court in
Ontario Human Rights Commission and O'Malley
v.
Simpsons-Sears Limited,

1985 CanLII 18 (SCC)
,
[1985] 2 S.C.R. 536
, 7 C.H.R.R. D/3102.

[
123
]  Discrimination by differential treatment (or direct discrimination, as it was referred to by McIntyre J.) occurs where an employer adopts a practice or rule which on its face discriminates on a prohibited ground. No intention to discriminate is required. McIntyre J. gave as an example, "No Catholics or no women or no blacks employed here." Other examples can be found in the case law to which McIntyre J. made reference.

(i)  In
Ontario Human Rights Commission
v.
Borough of Etobicoke,

1982 CanLII 15 (SCC)
,
[1982] 1 S.C.R. 202
, 3 C.H.R.R. D/781 a mandatory retirement provision contained in a collective agreement resulted in discrimination against those who had attained the stipulated age;

(ii)  In
Re Attorney-General for Alberta and Gares

(1976),
1976 CanLII 1116 (AB SCTD)
,
67 D.L.R. (3d) 635
a lower rate of pay for female employees than that for males resulted in discrimination against the former;

(iii)  In
British Columbia Human Rights Commission
v.
College of Physicians and Surgeons of B.C.,
(Bd. Inq. May 27, 1976) a policy adopted by the College which required doctors who were not Canadian citizens to practise in remote areas of the province was held to be discrimination because of nationality.

[
124
]  What all of these cases have in common is that the complainant was treated differently than others in respect of a term of employment (or licence to practice), because he or she fell into a different category than those others, a category on the basis of membership in which discrimination was prohibited.

[
125
]  Adverse effect discrimination was dealt with by the Supreme Court of Canada in
O'Malley, supra,
and in
Bhinder
v.
Canadian National Rlwy. Co.,

1985 CanLII 19 (SCC)
,
[1985] 2 S.C.R. 561
, 7 C.H.R.R. D/3093. It was said by McIntyre J. in
O'Malley,
at 551 [D/3106 at para. 24772 of C.H.R.R.], to arise:

. . . where an employer for genuine business reasons adopts a rule or standard which is on its face neutral, and which will apply equally to all employees, but which has a discriminatory effect upon a prohibited ground on one employee or group of employees in that it imposes, because of some special characteristic of the employee or group, obligations, penalties, or restrictive conditions not imposed on other members of the work force.

[
126
]  In both
O'Malley
and
Bhinder
a work rule of general application adversely affected the complainant because of a religious belief. It was not the adversity of effect alone which constituted the discrimination: it was discrimination because the adverse effect resulted from the complainants' religious belief, a categorical distinction between the complainants and other employees in each case.

[
127
]  The third way in which discrimination can occur, according to Professor Tarnopolsky (actually the first way described in his text), is where the complainant is treated differently from other employees with intent to distinguish the complainant categorically. I do not share his view that intent, as such, is ever an essential element of discrimination, but I will deal in this classification with discrimination in which the categorical basis of selection of a complainant must be proved by direct or circumstantial evidence. That will be the case only when neither the conduct of the employer nor its effect is discriminatory on its face as it was under the two classifications earlier considered.

[
128
]  I would dispense with intent as an essential element of discrimination for the reason given by McIntyre J. in
O'Malley
at 549 [D/3106 at para. 24768 of C.H.R.R.]:

To . . . hold that intent is a required element of discrimination . . . would seem to me to place a virtually insuperable barrier in the way of a complainant seeking a remedy.

The object of the
Act
is to eliminate discrimination which occurs whether it is intended or not. Proof of the ground on which the complainant was treated differently (the categorical distinction) cannot, however, be dispensed with as, without it, adverse treatment is not discrimination.

[
129
]  The word "discrimination" is sometimes used to mean "to distinguish unfavourably from others":
Oxford English Dictionary on Historical Principles.
In this sense it may have been used in legislation in other jurisdictions in which a categorical basis for discrimination is not required.

[
130
]  Under the
Canadian Human Rights Act,
S.C. 1976–77, c. 33, am. S.C. 1980–81–82–83, c. 143 a sanction is provided against anyone who engages in a discriminatory practice. A discriminatory practice includes, by express provision, harassment on a prohibited ground. The
Act
also provides that sexual harassment is to be deemed prohibited harassment. In the result, sexual harassment is discrimination. This is so not because it is, but because Parliament has said it shall be so.

[
131
]  Human rights legislation in other jurisdictions, such as Newfoundland, Ontario and Quebec, has recognized harassment as a wrong distinct from discrimination. The distinction may be of small importance as the complainant must still show that the harassment occurred because of a distinguishing feature, such as religion, race or sex. Nonetheless, the artifice of equating harassment with discrimination is avoided and a court can proceed directly to consider the cause of the harassment.

[
132
]  Harassment is as different from discrimination as assault is from random selection. The victim of assault may be chosen at random just as the victim of harassment may be chosen because of categorical distinction, but it is nonsense to say that assault is random selection just as it is nonsense to say that harassment is discrimination. The introduction of a sexual element, be it the nature of the conduct or the gender of the victim, does not alter the basic fact that harassment and assault are acts, whilst discrimination and random selection are methods of choice.

[
133
]  The fact that harassment is sexual in form does not determine the reason why the victim was chosen. Only if the woman was chosen on a categorical basis, without regard to individual characteristics, can the harassment be a manifestation of discrimination. Whether or not that is the case is a question of fact.

Sex

[
134
]  Gender, as distinct from the physical attraction of the victim or the manner in which the discrimination is carried out, is in my view the meaning to be given to "sex" as it is used in
section 6
of the
Act
.
Only in that sense does it constitute a category of persons as distinct from a personal quality. It is defined in the sense of "gender" in both
The Oxford Universal Dictionary on Historical Principles
(3rd ed.) and
Chambers' Twentieth Century Dictionary
(New Mid-Century ed.). It was also interpreted in this sense under similar legislation in Saskatchewan:
Re Board of Governors of the University of Saskatchewan and Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission

(1976),
1976 CanLII 1252 (SK QB)
,
66 D.L.R. (3d) 561
.

[
135
]  "Sex" can also refer to that aura which attracts one person to another, particular a person of one gender to a person of the other. In this meaning the word is frequently used in combination with another word, as in "sex appeal": see
Oxford Universal Dictionary on Historical Principles
(3rd ed.). The word in this sense, however, is not categorical in that the degree to which a person has it is determinable on a decidedly subjective basis.

[
136
]  Where the conduct of an employer is directed at some but not all persons of one category, it must not be assumed that membership of the category is the reason for the distinction having been made. The distinction may have been based upon another factor. Thus in
Bliss
v.
Attorney-General of Canada

(1978),
1978 CanLII 25 (SCC)
,
92 D.L.R. (3d) 417
it was held that statutory conditions applicable only to pregnant women did not discriminate against them as women. Ritchie J., delivering the judgment of the Court, adopted the reasons for the judgment of the Federal Court of Appeal [
1977 CanLII 3202 (FCA)
,
77 D.L.R. (3d) 609
] in which Pratte J., for the Court, said at 613:

Assuming the respondent to have been ”˜discriminated against', it would not have been by reason of her sex. Section 46 applies to pregnant women, it has no application to women who are not pregnant, and it has no application, of course, to men. If s. 46 treats unemployed pregnant women differently from other unemployed persons, be they male or female, it is, it seems to me, because they are pregnant and not because they are women.

[
137
]  The gender of a woman is unquestionably a factor in most cases of sexual harassment. If she were not a woman the harassment would not have occurred. That, however, is not decisive. Only a woman can become pregnant, but that does not mean that she becomes pregnant because she is a woman. We are concerned with the effective cause of the harassment, be it a random selection, the conduct, or a particular characteristic, of the victim, a wish on the part of the aggressor to discourage women from seeking or continuing in a position of employment or a contempt for women generally. Only in the last two instances is the harassment a manifestation of discrimination. The issue is thus reduced to a question of fact.

In Respect of Employment

[
138
]  To fall within the ambit of
section 6
of the
Act
,
conduct need not effect a change in the terms or conditions of employment. It is sufficient, in my view, that the conduct prejudices the employment opportunity in a direct way. Obviously a discriminatory attack on an individual on prohibited grounds by someone unconnected with the victim's employer would not be within the statute no matter what loss of employment opportunity resulted. The
Act
only prohibits conduct by or on behalf of the employer. This indicates the nature of a connection which must exist between the consequence of the conduct and the employment.

[
139
]  Co-employment of the discriminator and the victim is not by itself a sufficient connection. The extent to which an employee can be considered to be acting on behalf of the employer, in any particular case, must depend on the authority given, the position of the supervising employee within the employer's organization and the form of the allegedly discriminatory conduct. In the absence of proof of express authority, authority might still be inferred. In deciding the extent of the authority to be inferred, the scope of the supervisor's employment and the interest of the employer in having the supervisor do the things complained about must be considered. It will be more difficult to infer authority where the consequence of the supervisor's conduct is the loss of an experienced employee who will have to be replaced by a less experienced person from the same class as the employee who leaves (such as, a waitress having to be replaced by a waitress). The more personal the conduct alleged to be discriminatory, the more difficult it will be to infer that it was done on behalf of the employer. (See my comments on this point
in
Dakota Ojibway Tribal Council
v.
Bewza
, [1986] 2 W.W.R. at 235). The extent to which the employer has adopted the policy established by its supervisor will also be germane.

[
140
]  My view on this aspect of the case is supported by a majority of the Court in
Brennan
v.
Canada and Robichaud, supra.
Thurlow C. J., for himself and Pratte J., on this point, saw nothing in the
Canadian Human Rights Act,
S.C. 1976–77, c. 33, by which a person could be held liable for unauthorized discrimination by someone else. For my own part, I prefer to say that there is no discrimination in respect of employment where that which is alleged to be discriminatory was not authorized by the employer.

Other Case Law

[
141
]  Two Canadian appellate courts have considered the potential of sexual harassment as discrimination. In
Brennan
v.
Canada and Robichaud, supra,
the Federal Court of Appeal held that the question of whether or not the victim was harassed on a discriminatory basis because of sex was a question of fact.
In
Re Mehta and MacKinnon
, supra,
the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia held that a board of inquiry established under the
Human Rights Act
of Nova Scotia [1969 (N.S.) c.11] had jurisdiction to investigate a complaint of sexual harassment and consider whether or not, in the circumstances, it amounted to discrimination. Those decisions are in accord with the view I have expressed. To the extent that the opinions of the learned justices in either case purport to say more, I am not in accord with them.

[
142
]  Similarly, adjudicator O. B. Shime, Q. C.
in
Bell
and Korzak
v.
Ladas and The Flaming Steer Steak House, supra,
found the evidence insufficient to justify a finding that a violation of the
Ontario Human Rights Code
had occurred. He did say a great deal,
obiter,
as to the potential of sexual conduct as discrimination. Most of his comments were made on the assumption that the conduct was indulged in "because of sex", by which I understand him to have meant gender. To the extent that his comments were not made on that assumption, I disagree with him.

Application of the Law

[
143
]  In the present case both the board and the learned judge on appeal decided that the complainants were discriminated against. They did so, however, on the basis that sexual harassment is discrimination because of sex. For the reasons I have given, I am of the view that a finding of discrimination on that basis is wrong.

[
144
]  This is not a case in which an employer adopted a practice whereby women as a class were treated differently from men. Nor is it a case in which a rule of general application adversely affected the complainants because they were women. For the harassment to amount to discrimination, it must have occurred by reason of the categorical selection of the complainants because they were women.

[
145
]  Although not conclusive, the sex of the victims and the sexual nature of the harassment is some evidence of the basis of their selection. There is, on the other hand, no evidence that women as a class were not welcome as employees or were subject to adverse treatment. On the contrary, the evidence discloses that at the restaurant in question women were the only employees other than the cook and the corporate officer. Another female employee testified that the cook touched her a lot by putting his arm around her or touching her neck, but she interpreted that as him being friendly. She said that she and the cook got on fairly well: he treated her quite well. This evidence suggests that the complainants were chosen for the harassment because of characteristics peculiar to them rather than because of their sex. That is not discrimination no matter how objectionable the conduct.

[
146
]  Finally, because of the personal nature of the conduct and the fact that the employer could not gain by it, even in the achievement of a discriminatory goal, I do not consider that the victims were affected directly in respect of their employment. The board held that the employer condoned the cook's conduct. That is not, in my view, enough. Adoption of his conduct by the employer, not forgiveness, would be required at the very least to bring the cook's conduct within the meaning of the words "on behalf of the employer."

The Duty to Provide a Workplace Free of Harassment

[
147
]  An employer is liable to women discriminated against on its behalf. Wisdom dictates that an employer take steps to eradicate any discriminatory tendency on the part of its employees. There is, however, no requirement in the
Act
that an employer do so. In that circumstance, it is quite impossible to impose a legal duty on an employer to provide a workplace free of sexual harassment.

The Constitutional Issue

[
148
]  I am of the view that the power to confer jurisdiction on a tribunal to determine whether or not an employer had discriminated against a person in respect of his or her employment on a ground prohibited by the
Act
is
intra vires
a provincial legislature. The validity of any extension of that jurisdiction must depend on the nature of the additional jurisdiction conferred and the tribunal's function viewed as a whole. On my view of this case the board had jurisdiction to hear the complaint.

Damages

[
149
]  For the reasons given by my brother Huband, I am of the view that Monnin J. was right in reducing the quantum of damages.

Conclusion

[
150
]  In the result, I would allow the appeal of Platy and set aside the order of Monnin J. as well as the adjudication of the board. I would order that the Manitoba Human Rights Commission (which appeared to argue the case for the respondents) pay the costs of Platy in this court as well as in the Court of Queen's Bench and on the hearing before the board. I would assess the factum fee in this court at $100.00.
